original_value: AbstractPredictive modeling with electronic health record (EHR) data is anticipated to drive personalized medicine and improve healthcare quality. Constructing predictive statistical models typically requires extraction of curated predictor variables from normalized EHR data, a labor-intensive process that discards the vast majority of information in each patient’s record. We propose a representation of patients’ entire raw EHR records based on the Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) format. We demonstrate that deep learning methods using this representation are capable of accurately predicting multiple medical events from multiple centers without site-specific data harmonization. We validated our approach using de-identified EHR data from two US academic medical centers with 216,221 adult patients hospitalized for at least 24 h. In the sequential format we propose, this volume of EHR data unrolled into a total of 46,864,534,945 data points, including clinical notes. Deep learning models achieved high accuracy for tasks such as predicting: in-hospital mortality (area under the receiver operator curve [AUROC] across sites 0.93–0.94), 30-day unplanned readmission (AUROC 0.75–0.76), prolonged length of stay (AUROC 0.85–0.86), and all of a patient’s final discharge diagnoses (frequency-weighted AUROC 0.90). These models outperformed traditional, clinically-used predictive models in all cases. We believe that this approach can be used to create accurate and scalable predictions for a variety of clinical scenarios. In a case study of a particular prediction, we demonstrate that neural networks can be used to identify relevant information from the patient’s chart.

result.paraphrase: An abstract predictive modeling approach using electronic health record (EHR) data is expected to advance personalized medicine and enhance healthcare quality. Building predictive statistical models usually involves extracting curated predictor variables from normalized EHR data, a labor-intensive step that discards most of the information in each patient’s record. We introduce a patient representation based on the Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) format that captures the entirety of raw EHR records. Using this representation, we show that deep learning methods can accurately predict multiple medical events across multiple centers without site-specific data harmonization. Our approach was validated with de-identified EHR data from two US academic medical centers covering 216,221 adult patients hospitalized for at least 24 h. In the sequential format we propose, this amount of EHR data expanded into 46,864,534,945 total data points, including clinical notes. The deep learning models achieved strong performance on tasks including in-hospital mortality prediction (AUROC across sites 0.93–0.94), 30-day unplanned readmission (AUROC 0.75–0.76), prolonged length of stay (AUROC 0.85–0.86), and predicting all final discharge diagnoses for a patient (frequency-weighted AUROC 0.90). In every case, these models outperformed traditional predictive models used in clinical practice. We suggest that this method can support accurate, scalable predictions across a wide range of clinical scenarios. In a case study of one specific prediction task, we show that neural networks can identify relevant information from the patient’s chart.
